title: A DREAM FINISH ALLOWS AMERICA TO CARRY ON, DESPITE A ROTTEN CALL ON BALOGUN
text:
A DREAM FINISH ALLOWS AMERICA TO CARRY ON, DESPITE A ROTTEN CALL ON BALOGUN
The Americans overcame 35 minutes with only 10 players on the field, thanks to Malik Tillman’s free-kick goal, but a wicked red card could hurt their chances against Belgium on Monday night in Seattle
This was directly from the backyard, in America’s fantasies. Malik Tillman studied the biggest challenge in U.S. soccer history, stared at the goaltender, then kicked the ball mere inches over the breezed heads of five defenders. When it veered into the net, it meant the 250th anniversary of this nation’s existence will carry hope that the Round of 16 could spill into eight — or four, or two — on the World Cup bracket.
All while Folarin Balogun was the victim of an NBA referee, or Raphael Claus from Brazil, when he was ejected with a red card after his right foot injured the right ankle of an opponent. America is not supposed to be burned in America three days before a vital July 4, especially when Balogun will be suspended for at least the next game for his accidental act. At the moment, Tillman buried the call of serious foul play with poetry.
Taylor Swift is marrying Travis Kelce on Friday night at Madison Square Garden. The home soccer team won’t be playing Saturday, either, which is a monumental mistake in President Trump’s celebratory camp. How did Bosnia and Herzegovina not seize a one-man advantage for 35 minutes? Why was Balogun, who scored a first-half goal, deemed a villain when his play against Tarik Muharemovic should have been a caution instead of a VAR man’s dream? How did America play with 10 men against 11?
The wonder was answered by Tillman, whose free kick in the 82nd minute gave the U.S. a 2-0 victory and a Monday night match against beatable Belgium. Remember Curt Schilling and the famed bloody sock? Tillman had one too, fortunate that the equipment manager located a new right boot before his goal. Next thing you knew in Santa Clara, the country was singing along with John Denver — “Country Roads” — before Elvis Presley ramped up the speakers in with “Can’t Help Falling In Love.” The coach from small-town Argentina, Mauricio Pochettino, sang along in the same Hugo Boss outfit.
First, he wanted to mouth off about Balogun. “For me, never is it a red card,” Pochettino said. “It was a normal action in football that happened by accident. There was never any intention … and that is why, for me, it is never a red card.”
But then he saw a chance to be romantic. “So proud. The players deserve everything, and the way that we compete, there’s a lot to be proud, no?” he said. “So proud, so proud of all my players, all the staff, and then these fans, they are amazing again. It’s amazing to live that experience.”
Tillman echoed the thought. “Of course, I practiced it in training. And then, you never know when it’s gonna happen. Luckily, today it happened,” he said. “I was ready for it. I felt confident. I’m happy it went in. I think this shows our character. We’ve said it before a lot of times, we’re always there for each other no matter what. I think today showed that.”
Next up is Belgium, which struggled against Senegal before grasping the weight of circumstances and winning 3-2 in overtime. The U.S. won’t have Balogun, so the best of Christian Pulisic is needed against one of the world’s best goalies, Thibaut Courtois. Analysts will discuss the red card for days. “Absolute BS,’’ Fox’s Landon Donovan said. Still, the darlings will have another boisterous crowd in Seattle. Why lose now? This was the first time in 11 matches when America beat a European team. Belgium also is from Europe and has plenty of issues.
“We had to dig deep for that one,” Pulisic said. “We didn’t deserve the red card. It was unfortunate. But that’s what (Tillman) does. It was special. To see it go in was amazing. We said in the hydration break, you know, this is what it takes to be a really strong team. And we were able to do it.”
For the longest time, the enemy coach was so angry that he held the ball for too long. Sergej Barbarez was convinced the officials were allowing the U.S. to win despite Balogun’s absence. Never mind. This is the first time America has won three games at a World Cup. “I think it shows how strong the team is. We went down a man, and nobody really stressed out,” defender Chris Richards said. “It was unlucky for Flo (Balogun), but it is what it is. So we got on with it, and it was very important we kept a clean sheet, and then the cherry on top was Malik’s free kick.”
Fox is rooting for the U.S., naturally. But consider these comments when weighing the red card. “This is not consistent with what I’ve seen the rest of this tournament,” former Premier League referee Mark Clattenburg said on the broadcast. “When this type of challenge comes, it’s more of a stepping action, and when it’s a stepping action it lacks force and aggression. The problem you have is when he puts his foot down, he puts it down on the foot of the Bosnia and Herzegovina player. So that’s what creates the movement down and creates the ankle twist. So does it endanger the safety of the opponent? You could argue it does, but I think it’s unfair because it’s more of a stepping action.”
Unfair, he said. We don’t need a lack of reason in the World Cup. The Americans deserve the Round of 16. If they lose Monday because of Balogun, why play soccer?
###
Jay Mariotti, called “without question the most impacting Chicago sportswriter of the past quarter-century,’’ writes general sports columns for Substack while appearing on some of the 1,678,498 podcasts and shows in production today. He is an accomplished columnist, TV panelist and talk/podcast host.
